title: What International Tests Can Tell Us About How To Improve Education
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler reviews Improving a Country's Education, a book edited by Nuno Crato that analyses PISA 2018 results in ten countries. She argues the data challenge progressive orthodoxy: Finland's decline after 2006 may reflect a shift away from a centralised, explicit-instruction system, and Estonia, the new top performer, has a demanding curriculum and more teacher-led instruction. Crato's PISA analysis links teacher-directed teaching with higher science scores, and the evidence suggests it works especially well for students with little prior knowledge and from lower-income backgrounds. National tests alone do not help, as the Spanish and American cases show, without remediation. Her conclusion, echoing Crato, is that everything starts with curriculum: what is taught and how.
points: Finland's post-2006 decline invites the possibility that its earlier explicit-instruction system, not progressive reform, produced its success.
Estonia combines a demanding content curriculum, school autonomy, a culture of self-criticism and more explicit instruction than peers.
PISA data correlate teacher-led instruction with higher science scores and student-centred approaches with lower ones.
Testing without remediation does not improve equity, as the Spanish and American experiences show.
Reformers should turn to the neglected levers of what is taught and how it is delivered.
quotes: After the first administration of the PISA in 2000, Finland’s top ranking turned it into a beacon of hope for other countries, including the U.S. So-called “edutourists” flocked to the country in hopes of discovering its secret education sauce.

But in 2006, Finland’s PISA scores began a steady and significant decline. And some have pointed out that there’s a time lag between the adoption of education policy and the performance of 15-year-olds on tests.

One little-noticed result of the 2018 PISA, at least in the U.S., was the emergence of Estonia as the new Finland. The country came out at or near the top on all three subjects—math, reading, and science—and has done relatively well in narrowing the test-score gaps between socioeconomic groups.

As Crato notes, it’s not that teacher-directed instruction is always best. But there’s quite a bit of evidence that it’s far more efficient when students have little preexisting knowledge about a topic.

In her chapter, Spanish education expert Montse Gomendio argues that the lack of national tests in that country has led to serious inequity: struggling students can’t be identified and given remediation, and the result is a huge number of students who are forced to repeat a grade because they can’t keep up with the work.

Perhaps the lesson of the American experience is that—as Crato says in his introduction—“everything starts with curriculum.” Tests won’t accomplish much without a content-rich, rigorous curriculum in place—and pedagogical approaches that are tailored to the knowledge and skills of students.
